title: Jailer 2: Critics Say Rajinikanth's Swagger Carries a Sequel That Runs Out of Plot
excerpt: Reviewers split the film in two — a rollicking, comedy-rich first half powered by the Superstar, and a second half where the writing stops keeping up with him.
body:
• Critics score Jailer 2 between 2.5 and 3.5 out of 5 — a near-unanimous split verdict: strong first half, weak second
  • Rajinikanth's screen presence and the Namo Narayana–Yogi Babu comedy track are praised by every major outlet
  • Anirudh's background score is a highlight; his songs are not
  • The villain tracks and star cameos are widely judged to add bulk, not impact, in a nearly three-hour runtime

Three years after Tiger Muthuvel Pandian walked out of retirement and into one of Tamil cinema's biggest hits, the sequel arrives with the same bet the first film made: that Rajinikanth, doing less, means more. Set three months after the events of Jailer, Nelson Dilipkumar's film finds syndicates hunting for the men who killed Varma and for his missing fortune, and the trail leads back to the quiet house where Muthuvel is trying to stay retired. Critics agree the setup works — for about half the film. What follows is the most consistent split verdict of the season: nearly every major review praises the same first half and faults the same second one.

The disagreement is only about degree. Filmfare, awarding the film 3 out of 5, calls it an entertaining sequel in which Rajinikanth's charisma and Nelson's dark humour do the heavy lifting, while Telugu Cinema's Jalapathy Gudelli, at 2.5 out of 5, concludes that Nelson relies more on Rajini's swag than on strong writing. Between those poles — CineTalkers at the generous end with 3.5, 123telugu in the middle with 3 — the same film keeps appearing: a star vehicle whose engine is superb and whose chassis creaks.

The consensus

Across the published reviews, Jailer 2 scores cluster tightly between 2.5 and 3.5 out of 5, and the shape of the notices is remarkably uniform. The first half is described as playful and comedy-forward, built around Tiger's plan taking shape and Nelson letting his supporting cast breathe; the second half, once the syndicates and the villain tracks take over, is where reviewers say the screenplay thins out into familiar mass-movie beats — star elevations and exaggerated action where a compelling conflict should be. LukMyShow's reading of six published reviews, which ranged from 2.5 to 3.5, lands at 2.9 — and that is about where the consensus sits: a sequel that entertains in stretches, carried by its star, let down by its writing.

What's praised

Rajinikanth himself, first and unanimously. Filmfare writes that he brings effortless authority to Tiger without having to dominate every scene, and that his comic timing complements Nelson's irreverent sensibility. 123telugu notes that the walk, the slow removal of the glasses and the screen presence still draw strong reactions from the crowd — the star, now fifty years into his career, carrying the role comfortably. Telugu Cinema's Gudelli is blunter: Rajinikanth is terrific again, and whenever he is on screen, his presence commands attention; much of the film's entertainment comes from that presence rather than the writing.

The comedy ensemble draws the next loudest praise. Filmfare singles out Namo Narayana as Moorthi, whose equation with Yogi Babu provides some of the film's funniest moments, and credits Nelson for finding humour in the characters' responses rather than forcing punchlines. 123telugu likewise notes the first half leans heavily on comedy that lands, with Namo Narayana given plenty of room. Among the antagonists, Vidya Balan's turn in a negative role is repeatedly called effective — a change from her usual parts, handled well — while S. J. Suryah handles the main antagonist's duties in his familiar, reliable style. And Anirudh Ravichander's background score is praised across outlets as one of the film's strengths, elevating the hero moments even where his songs do not register.

What's criticized

The second half is the charge sheet. Telugu Cinema says Nelson slips into familiar mass-movie territory once the main conflict unfolds, depending on star elevations instead of building a real confrontation, so the emotional moments land softly. Reviewers tracking the audience response, Venky Reviews among them, describe the S. J. Suryah and Vidya Balan villain tracks as tiring and short on impact, and the much-discussed cameos — Mohanlal and Shiva Rajkumar return, with Hrithik Roshan appearing — as plot devices rather than genuine high points. Filmfare's gentler version of the same complaint is an overcrowded screenplay: the film's ambitions eventually get the better of its storytelling. At just under three hours, the length works against it; more than one review notes sequences that feel overstretched as the film moves away from the entertainment that works best.

What this means for you

For diaspora audiences, this is the easiest ticket of the month and the hardest to love completely. It is playing in Tamil with Telugu and Hindi dubbed versions, and Rajinikanth's opening has already been a phenomenon — the film posted one of the biggest worldwide openings of his career, so the theatrical crowd experience is half the fun. Go for the first half, the comedy, and a superstar doing what only he does; keep expectations for the back half modest. Amazon Prime Video is reported to hold the streaming rights, though no date has been announced.

data_cards.rating_consensus: Critics converge on a 3-star verdict: a rollicking first half built on Rajinikanth's swagger, Nelson's dark comedy and Anirudh's score, followed by an overcrowded second half where the writing stops keeping up — good fun, short of the first film.
